hints.hint: Turn every condition, including what a person says about what they know, into an explicit constraint on your unknowns: divisibility, an inequality, a bound, a count. Impose them in the order spoken. If some quantity's role is left ambiguous and no single reading lets a speaker be uncertain, uncertainty needs several readings live at once: intersect their constraints on that speaker's own value rather than testing each reading alone and rejecting all. A contradiction is a deduction, not a dead end -- it kills one assumption you added, so note which died and move on; never restart or re-derive a settled case. Never import a remembered value from a similar-looking classic puzzle, and never pick a candidate because it looks intended or is merely the smallest -- write each condition out and check it. Commit to your result early, verify once, stop.

Divide by the appropriate power of the variable to introduce the ratio w=(z-1)/z; the equation then pins w to a finite set on a circle. Solve for z in terms of w and turn the locus into an equation in x and y, completing the square to read off center and radius. Generally: substitute so the relation depends on one quantity, and keep every value exact.

A spot-check that disagrees with your derivation almost always means arithmetic inside the check, not a broken problem. Recheck that one line only; never restart from scratch or declare the setup inconsistent. Two exact points plus a symmetry axis pin a circle faster than solving a large linear system. State your simplified result as soon as you have one, then use leftover room to confirm it.

Fix one setup and never rebuild it. Overlapping pieces obey total = sum minus overlap, so maximize coverage by minimizing overlap; the same bookkeeping serves counting. A corner reaches only the directions inside its own angle, so what it covers of the small piece is a wedge: part of that piece always lies outside, part always inside. The overlap is therefore strictly between zero and the whole piece; both extreme claims are wrong. Settle the free parameter by a trade, not by sampling: shift it slightly and compare what enters the overlap against what leaves. Matched pieces mean the quantity never moved, so no further value can teach you anything. End reasoning there, do the sum-minus-overlap arithmetic in your first visible line, and state the result next. Never append a section asking whether another configuration wins.

For "at most how many" questions give both halves: an upper bound and an example reaching it. Name a count early, before you run long.

Posit ONE unknown affine target for the whole pattern (an arithmetic progression is A+B*n), shared by every piece. Index n is usable by piece f exactly when the residual f(x)-(A+Bx) vanishes at n. Never demand that one piece alone give consecutive terms; neighbours may come from different pieces, and that false demand makes the task look impossible.

A nonzero degree-d residual has at most d roots - but that caps ONE piece, not the pattern. Pieces are reusable, each with its own residual and disjoint root set, so budgets ADD over all m pieces: total <= m*d.

Before stopping, check your count uses every number given; if it is only the degree, or only the piece count, you dropped a factor.

Attain the bound with consecutive blocks, one piece each.

Name your unknowns and turn each given condition into one exact equation; solve for any constants first. Reduce to a single variable, keep exact fractions, and discard roots that are degenerate or outside the domain. Verify a candidate by substituting it back into the original conditions, not by re-deriving; once it passes, stop revisiting it. Re-read the question and report the exact quantity it asks for, simplified. State your result early, then stop.

Trap: asserting symmetry. "Each item is equally likely in any position", or "n! orderings so 1/n!", is a guess. A process random over MOVES is rarely uniform over OUTCOMES.

Build ONE sample space and reuse it for EVERY part. Its atoms are the genuinely FREE 50/50 choices: a step is 1/2 only when both options are legal, forced steps count 1, giving 2^(free) atoms — not 2^(all moves), not n!.

Before counting, settle the asked slot. Write BOTH readings — that slot holds the FIRST arrival, or the LAST — then kill one by tracing a single concrete run to the end under the stated placement rule. Never carry an unchecked reading into a count.

Each part is then (atoms meeting its constraint)/2^(free). Never divide a permutation count by a branch count, and never retreat to 1/n.

Reach a stated result early, then spend the rest of your effort checking it: reasoning that never lands scores nothing. Take the cheapest concrete foothold first -- at a large or symbolic size, work the smallest honest instances out exactly, substitute back to confirm each, and match the confirmed values against factorials, binomials, powers, and simple products, watching sign and any off-by-one shift. Once you hold concrete numbers, that is the route you finish. Switching to a slicker representation mid-solve is the classic way to lose: a reformulation that introduces unknowns the stated conditions cannot fix is a worse description of the problem, not a deeper one -- drop it and extend your table by one more instance. If one value breaks a pattern the rest obey, recheck its arithmetic rather than retheorizing.

Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, and apply the stated markup multiplicatively. In general, when a direct attack stalls, work the smallest cases by hand and read off the pattern or invariant rather than pushing a long computation. Keep quantities exact as fractions or products and simplify only at the close. State your result plainly as soon as you have it, then check it once.

Never name a full set of unknown coefficients and never expand a composed or high-degree identity; that exhausts your budget. Recenter: put both maps about one shared unknown center c, f=c+a(x-c)^k and g=c-a(x-c)^k with odd k, so the identity collapses by symmetry. Take the opposite-sign branch first; same-sign is degenerate. Carry no extra offset and never factor c out. The two supplied values are then c-a*c^k and c+a*c^k: adding them must cancel the a-term, leaving one linear equation for c; subtracting isolates a. A quadratic or irrational center means your signs are wrong: fix that one line, never by expanding. Ask whether a requested input equals c or a fixed point, making its value immediate. Verify by symmetry, commit, state your result early, and stop re-deriving.

Prefer literal computation to compact notation. Run the stated procedure on the smallest instance step by step, each step acting on the previous step's output, never on the original data, and write the whole state after each step. That worked run outranks everything else. When a formula, a tidier notation, or a claim about structure disagrees with it, do not repair the model and do not suspect the run: drop that language entirely and finish by plain repetition, applying the whole procedure again and again and counting. You owe no decomposition and no general proof. Then let the requested form police the result: an expression in a parameter must move with that parameter, and the smallest instance you trust must satisfy it; if it does not, shift the exponent, not the instance. Calling the setup confusing, or repeating a line, means stop and state the value your instances support.
